Dynamic Effects in Longitudinal AME Models

Cassy Dorff, Tosin Salau, Shahryar Minhas

2026-11-20

Source: vignettes/articles/dynamic_effects.Rmd
dynamic_effects.Rmd

Introduction

Networks change. Allies drift apart, tastes evolve. The standard AME model pools across time, assuming each actor has a fixed latent position and fixed additive effects in every period. The lame package provides three mechanisms for relaxing that assumption: dynamic_uv for time-varying latent positions, dynamic_ab for time-varying additive effects, and dynamic_beta for time-varying regression coefficients. This vignette explains what each option does, when to use it, and how to interpret the results.

What Are Dynamic Effects?

The Static Baseline

In the standard AME model for longitudinal data, the tie between actors ii and jj at time tt is:

yij,t=β′xij,t+ai+bj+ui′vj+ϵij,ty_{ij,t} = \beta'x_{ij,t} + a_i + b_j + u_i'v_j + \epsilon_{ij,t}

The covariates (xij,tx_{ij,t}) can vary over time, but the sender effect aia_i, the receiver effect bjb_j, and the latent positions uiu_i and vjv_j are constant: the model assumes a country’s position in the latent “sanctioning space” is the same in 1993 as in 2000.

Dynamic Latent Positions (dynamic_uv = TRUE)

When you set dynamic_uv = TRUE, each actor’s latent position evolves over time according to an AR(1) process:

Ui,k,t=ρuvUi,k,t−1+ϵi,k,t,ϵi,k,t∼N(0,σuv2)U_{i,k,t} = \rho_{uv} \, U_{i,k,t-1} + \epsilon_{i,k,t}, \quad \epsilon_{i,k,t} \sim N(0, \sigma_{uv}^2)Vj,k,t=ρuvVj,k,t−1+ηj,k,t,ηj,k,t∼N(0,σuv2)V_{j,k,t} = \rho_{uv} \, V_{j,k,t-1} + \eta_{j,k,t}, \quad \eta_{j,k,t} \sim N(0, \sigma_{uv}^2)

Note the innovation parameterisation: σuv2\sigma_{uv}^2 is the variance of the period-to-period innovation, not the marginal/stationary variance of Ui,k,tU_{i,k,t} (which is σuv2/(1−ρuv2)\sigma_{uv}^2 / (1 - \rho_{uv}^2)), and fit$sigma_uv holds posterior draws of the innovation standard deviation. For symmetric fits it is not estimated: the unit-variance gauge fixes σuv=1−ρuv2\sigma_{uv} = \sqrt{1 - \rho_{uv}^2}, and fit$sigma_uv is that function of the ρuv\rho_{uv} draws. The autoregressive parameter ρuv\rho_{uv}, estimated from the data, controls persistence: near 1 means positions change slowly, near 0 means they are essentially re-drawn each period. Use this when the underlying community structure is evolving – alliances shift, trading blocs realign.

Dynamic Additive Effects (dynamic_ab = TRUE)

When you set dynamic_ab = TRUE, each sender and receiver effect is a per-actor level plus a zero-mean AR(1) deviation:

ai,t=μia+di,t,di,t=ρabdi,t−1+ϵi,t,ϵi,t∼N(0,σab2)a_{i,t} = \mu^{a}_{i} + d_{i,t}, \quad d_{i,t} = \rho_{ab} \, d_{i,t-1} + \epsilon_{i,t}, \quad \epsilon_{i,t} \sim N(0, \sigma_{ab}^2)bj,t=μjb+ej,t,ej,t=ρabej,t−1+ηj,t,ηj,t∼N(0,σab2)b_{j,t} = \mu^{b}_{j} + e_{j,t}, \quad e_{j,t} = \rho_{ab} \, e_{j,t-1} + \eta_{j,t}, \quad \eta_{j,t} \sim N(0, \sigma_{ab}^2)

The level μia\mu^{a}_{i} is pooled over every period, and its variance across actors is the va that summary() reports (vb for the receiver levels). The deviation carries the dynamics: fit$rho_ab is its persistence and fit$sigma_ab holds draws of its innovation standard deviation, with the stationary variance σab2/(1−ρab2)\sigma_{ab}^2 / (1 - \rho_{ab}^2) as the prior on the first-period deviation. The marginal variance of a per-period effect is therefore σa2+σab2/(1−ρab2)\sigma^2_a + \sigma_{ab}^2 / (1 - \rho_{ab}^2), and because ρab\rho_{ab} describes movement around a level, on short panels it reads lower than the persistence of the raw effect path. Unless you set prior$sigma_ab_scale, its scale is fixed before sampling from the prior mean of the active level variances and prior$rho_ab_mean, so per-period deviations shrink toward the actor’s level unless the data insist; on sparse binary panels this is what keeps the effects from chasing single cells. The stored paths fit$a_dynamic and fit$b_dynamic are the full effects ai,ta_{i,t} and bj,tb_{j,t}. Substantively, dynamic_ab captures changes in how much an actor participates, not in who they connect with (that is dynamic_uv’s territory). The two can be used alone or together; dynamic_ab is often the place to start, since changes in overall activity are common and relatively easy to estimate.

The effects of every period sum to zero across actors, so a shift common to all actors in one period (the whole network busier in period tt) cannot sit in them. Under dynamic_ab = TRUE the intercept therefore becomes a dynamic coefficient automatically (a dynamic_beta block of its own, added to whatever dynamic_beta names, and a random walk unless dynamic_beta_kind is "rw2" or "matern32", so its forecasts hold the last level), and it carries the period means: fit$BETA is then a draws x coefficients x periods array and coef(fit)["intercept", ] is the intercept path. fit$dynamic_intercept_from_ab records that the rule applied.

Dynamic Regression Coefficients (dynamic_beta)

The third option lets the regression coefficients themselves evolve. With dynamic_beta = TRUE (or a subset like dynamic_beta = "dyad"), each selected coefficient follows an AR(1) around its own long-run mean μk\mu_k:

βk,t−μk=ρβ,b(k)(βk,t−1−μk)+ϵk,t,ϵk,t∼N(0,σβ,b(k)2Λkk)\beta_{k,t} - \mu_k = \rho_{\beta,b(k)} \, (\beta_{k,t-1} - \mu_k) + \epsilon_{k,t}, \quad \epsilon_{k,t} \sim N(0, \sigma_{\beta,b(k)}^2 \Lambda_{kk})

where b(k)b(k) is the block of coefficient kk (intercept / dyad / row / col), so coefficients in a block share ρ\rho and σ\sigma, while the design-based scale Λkk\Lambda_{kk} (a gg-prior analogue) keeps each innovation variance commensurate with the data. The first period is drawn from the stationary law around μk\mu_k, and μk\mu_k has the prior of a static coefficient; its posterior is in fit$mu_beta and fit$MU_BETA, and forecasts of the coefficient revert to it. The whole time path of β\beta is drawn jointly via forward-filter / backward-sample (FFBS; Carter & Kohn 1994). One storage difference from dynamic_uv / dynamic_ab: fit$sigma_beta and fit$rho_beta hold last-iteration scalars, while the full posterior draws live in fit$SIGMA_BETA and fit$RHO_BETA – summarise those (e.g. colMeans(fit$SIGMA_BETA)).

dynamic_beta accepts FALSE (default), TRUE (all coefficients), block shortcuts ("intercept", "dyad", "row", "col") or coefficient names, integer column indices, or a length-p logical mask; see ?lame. When the intercept (or a nodal coefficient) is dynamic, an automatic sum-to-zero constraint on a (and b) keeps everything jointly identified. dynamic_beta works for every family, unipartite and bipartite, directed and symmetric, and combines with dynamic_ab / dynamic_uv.

A worked dynamic_beta example

Simulate a small longitudinal network where a single dyadic covariate’s effect grows linearly over time, and fit with dynamic_beta = "dyad".

library(lame)
set.seed(2026)

n_db <- 15
T_db <- 5
beta_t_true <- seq(-0.5, 1.0, length.out = T_db) # truth: rising effect

X_db <- replicate(T_db, matrix(rnorm(n_db * n_db), n_db, n_db), simplify = FALSE)
Y_db <- vector("list", T_db)
for (t in seq_len(T_db)) {
    Yt <- beta_t_true[t] * X_db[[t]] + matrix(rnorm(n_db * n_db, 0, 0.4), n_db, n_db)
    diag(Yt) <- NA
    rownames(Yt) <- colnames(Yt) <- paste0("a", seq_len(n_db))
    Y_db[[t]] <- Yt
}
names(Y_db) <- paste0("t", seq_len(T_db))
X_db_arr <- lapply(X_db, function(x) array(x, c(n_db, n_db, 1)))

fit_db <- lame(
    Y_db,
    Xdyad = X_db_arr,
    family = "normal",
    R = 0,
    nscan = 200,
    burn = 50,
    odens = 5,
    dynamic_beta = "dyad",
    verbose = FALSE
)

# fit$BETA is an [n_stored x p x T] array
dim(fit_db$BETA)
#> [1] 80  2  5

# coef() gives a p x T matrix of posterior means
coef(fit_db)
#>                     t1           t2           t3           t4           t5
#> intercept -0.008732057 -0.008732057 -0.008732057 -0.008732057 -0.008732057
#> X1_dyad   -0.487500970 -0.124287971  0.229302499  0.632750708  0.989391697

# 95% credible intervals, one row per coefficient and period
head(confint(fit_db), 8)
#>                      2.5%       97.5%
#> intercept[t1] -0.03344747  0.01328026
#> X1_dyad[t1]   -0.55017014 -0.43839113
#> intercept[t2] -0.03344747  0.01328026
#> X1_dyad[t2]   -0.18066401 -0.07348713
#> intercept[t3] -0.03344747  0.01328026
#> X1_dyad[t3]    0.17742945  0.28710450
#> intercept[t4] -0.03344747  0.01328026
#> X1_dyad[t4]    0.59086680  0.67738465

Reading the coefficients. With dynamic_beta active, fit$BETA is a 3-D [n_stored, p, T] array, one slice per period. coef(fit) summarises it: a [p, T] matrix of posterior means for a dynamic fit and a length-p vector for a static one, so the same call works on both. To summarise the draws by hand, keep the period dimension: apply(fit$BETA, c(2, 3), mean).

The posterior means for X1_dyad follow the simulated ramp beta_t_true = c(-0.5, -0.125, 0.25, 0.625, 1.0): the largest gap between the two over the five periods is 0.021.

Choosing a prior family: dynamic_beta_kind

lame() exposes dynamic_beta_kind for selecting the prior family on the time-varying coefficients:

Mean-reverting coefficient? Use the default dynamic_beta_kind = "ar1". Permanent / unit-root drift (no mean reversion)? Use "rw1". Smooth with curvature (second-order smoothness)? Use "rw2". Smooth with a known length-scale of variation? Use "matern32" (set the scale via prior = list(matern32_length_scale = ...); defaults to max(2, T/4)). After an AR(1) fit, summary(fit) checks the posterior on ρβ\rho_\beta and recommends "rw1" when it is concentrated at or above 0.97 ("rw2" if acceleration matters).

"random_walk" is an alias for "rw1". "rw2" and "matern32" draw the whole path in one joint Gaussian update; ?lame gives their cost per iteration. Refitting fit_db under each kind and comparing the recovered X1_dyad path against the truth:

kinds <- c("rw1", "rw2", "matern32")
paths <- sapply(kinds, function(k) {
    fit_k <- lame(
        Y_db,
        Xdyad = X_db_arr,
        family = "normal",
        R = 0,
        nscan = 200,
        burn = 50,
        odens = 5,
        dynamic_beta = "dyad",
        dynamic_beta_kind = k,
        prior = if (k == "matern32")
            list(matern32_length_scale = 2) else NULL,
        verbose = FALSE
    )
    coef(fit_k)["X1_dyad", ]
})
round(
    rbind(
        ar1 = coef(fit_db)["X1_dyad", ],
        t(paths),
        truth = beta_t_true
    ),
    3
)
#>              t1     t2    t3    t4    t5
#> ar1      -0.488 -0.124 0.229 0.633 0.989
#> rw1      -0.488 -0.122 0.228 0.637 0.986
#> rw2      -0.476 -0.133 0.230 0.626 0.993
#> matern32 -0.482 -0.124 0.228 0.630 0.987
#> truth    -0.500 -0.125 0.250 0.625 1.000

All four kinds recover the ramp: the largest gap between any estimate in the table and the truth is 0.024. On a smooth, evenly spaced trend the priors agree in-sample; they separate when the data have the feature each one models (mean reversion, permanent drift, curvature), so choose with the decision list above.

When time_index is supplied with unequal gaps, the AR(1) / RW1 conditional variance is scaled by the gap (suppressing Λkk\Lambda_{kk} for readability): qt=σβ2⋅1−ρβ2Δt1−ρβ2q_t = \sigma_\beta^2 \cdot \frac{1 - \rho_\beta^{2\Delta_t}}{1 - \rho_\beta^2} so quarterly-then-annual data gets the correct prior; "rw2" and "matern32" support unequal gaps through their joint precision-matrix construction.

# observation times 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 (doubling gaps)
fit_gaps <- lame(
    Y_db,
    Xdyad = X_db_arr,
    family = "normal",
    R = 0,
    nscan = 200,
    burn = 50,
    odens = 5,
    dynamic_beta = "dyad",
    time_index = c(1, 2, 4, 8, 16)[seq_len(T_db)],
    verbose = FALSE
)
fit_gaps$time_index
#> [1]  1  2  4  8 16
round(coef(fit_gaps), 3)
#>               t1     t2     t3     t4     t5
#> intercept -0.014 -0.014 -0.014 -0.014 -0.014
#> X1_dyad   -0.480 -0.125  0.232  0.638  0.991

Hierarchical pooling: dynamic_beta_pool

When two or more coefficient blocks are dynamic, each block has its own AR(1) hyperparameters by default. On a short panel (T≤5T \le 5) a single block carries little information about its own persistence and innovation scale, and dynamic_beta_pool lets the blocks share it by shrinking the block-level hyperparameters toward a common mean: "rho" for common persistence, "sigma" for a common innovation scale, "both" for full pooling – e.g. lame(..., dynamic_beta = c("intercept", "dyad"), dynamic_beta_pool = "both"). With a single dynamic block the hierarchical layer is skipped entirely and the fit is identical to the default "none". See ?lame for the diagnostic comparison of pooled vs independent hyperparameter posteriors.

Per-actor time-varying slopes: dynamic_beta_per_actor

For questions about whether one actor responds to a covariate differently than another – and whether that gap evolves – set dynamic_beta_per_actor = "row" (or "col") and pick the covariate via per_actor_covariate_idx, e.g. lame(..., dynamic_beta_per_actor = "row", per_actor_covariate_idx = 1L). Deviations are sum-to-zero centred at every period, so the population coefficient stays in coef(fit) while the per-actor deviations land in fit$THETA_ACTOR (and their posterior means in fit$theta_actor_mean, labelled by actor and period). See ?per_actor_slopes.

Diagnosing your dynamic fit

summary(fit) prints the Dynamic coefficients per period block and the per-block posterior-mean rho_beta, and recommends dynamic_beta_kind = "rw1" when a block’s posterior on ρβ\rho_\beta is concentrated at or above 0.97.

detect_change_point(fit) is a path diagnostic. It scales each coefficient’s largest one-period change by its fitted innovation standard deviation, including the covariate-design scale, and compares it with reference paths that have the same number of periods, start from the first state of the same posterior draw and follow its persistence and innovation scale. The bf column is a tail ratio between zero and twenty, not a Bayes factor. At the default threshold_bf it flagged at most 5% of simulated panels whose coefficient followed a smooth path or the fitted law, and a step of 1.2 in most panels of eight or more periods but in about a fifth of those with four or five (?detect_change_point gives the rates by panel length).

detect_change_point(fit_db)
#>      coef bf m_post_mean m_prior_q95 t_hat  warn
#> 1 X1_dyad  0    1.460523    2.765587     4 FALSE

The ramp in fit_db is smooth, and the output says so: warn is FALSE. Use large tail ratios to select paths for closer inspection; t_hat is the period in which the largest jump most often falls. The reference paths are defined for equally spaced AR(1) and RW1 coefficients. For prior elicitation before fitting, dynamic_beta_prior_summary(n_periods = 10, kind = "ar1") simulates coefficient paths from the prior on ρβ\rho_\beta and σβ\sigma_\beta, with Λkk=1\Lambda_{kk} = 1.

fit$sampler_health counts, for each sampler step, the proposals that fell outside a prior bound (prior$uv_max_abs, prior$G_max). These are ordinary Metropolis rejections, and summary() states their share of sweeps when it is one percent or more. Its numerical_failures column is zero in every returned fit. Between-chain agreement and effective sample sizes are in fit$rhat, described below.

Temporal-trend posterior-predictive check: gof_temporal()

Where detect_change_point() targets coefficients, gof_temporal(fit, stat = "density", n_rep = 200) targets the network statistic itself: it fits a linear time trend to a chosen statistic (density / mean / reciprocity / transitivity), computes the same slope on simulate(fit) replicates, and returns a two-sided posterior-predictive p-value; small p_pp (below 0.05) means the observed trend is incompatible with the fitted model. Reach for it when the substantive statistic drifts across the panel; the overview vignette has a worked example, and ?gof_temporal the reference.

Inspecting the priors actually in effect: prior_summary()

prior_summary(fit) prints the hyperparameters actually used, defaults filled in – for a dynamic fit that includes the per-block AR(1) priors alongside the variance components and the g-prior on beta. Run it once per fit to confirm that a prior = list(...) override took effect; see ?prior_summary and the cross-sectional vignette for the general tour.

Multi-chain R̂\hat R via lame_parallel() and rhat_dynamic_beta()

lame() runs two chains by default and compares them before it returns: fit$rhat lists the R̂\hat R and effective draws of every monitored quantity. For a statistic on the whole per-period coefficient path, fit several chains with lame_parallel(..., n_chains = 4, combine_method = "list") and call rhat_dynamic_beta() on the resulting list. It returns rhat_mvt, a multivariate statistic that catches chains agreeing period by period while disagreeing on the trajectory, and rhat_max_univariate; quote a path when both are below 1.01. For the fit_db model, four chains of the default length give rhat_mvt = 1.003 and rhat_max_univariate = 1.001 for X1_dyad. combine_ame_chains() pools chains and routes through posterior::summarise_draws() for per-(coefficient, period) ESS. ame_parallel() is the cross-sectional twin; see ?rhat_dynamic_beta, ?lame_parallel, and the cross-sectional vignette.

Forecasting

predict(fit, h = K) propagates the joint posterior state forward KK periods, retaining uncertainty in the paths and their hyperparameters. Each coefficient is forecast by its own kind on equally spaced periods: an AR(1) coefficient reverts to its long-run mean, an RW1 coefficient holds its last level, an RW2 coefficient extends its last slope and a Matern 3/2 coefficient returns toward zero over its length scale. Per-actor slopes (dynamic_beta_per_actor) describe the fitted periods. The forecasting vignette covers forecast scales, per-draw arrays, credible intervals, counterfactual covariates, exposure offsets and the choice between AR(1) and RW1.

Visualising the coefficient path: autoplot.lame

For a fit with dynamic_beta active, autoplot(fit) returns a ggplot ribbon plot per coefficient (posterior median line, 95% interval, faceted by coefficient). Under dynamic_beta = "dyad" the intercept remains static, so pass coefs = to restrict the plot to the genuinely time-varying coefficients:

library(ggplot2)
autoplot(fit_db, coefs = "X1_dyad", probs = c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975)) +
    labs(
        title = "Posterior coefficient path",
        subtitle = "Median line, 95% credible interval ribbon",
        x = "Time period", y = "Coefficient value"
    )

LOO / WAIC via save_log_lik = TRUE

Pass save_log_lik = TRUE and lame attaches a [n_stored, n_obs] pointwise log-likelihood matrix to fit$log_lik, which loo::loo(fit) and loo::waic(fit) read directly. The example fits independent residuals (dcor = FALSE), so each observed cell is one likelihood factor:

fit_ll <- lame(
    Y_db,
    Xdyad = X_db_arr,
    family = "normal",
    R = 0,
    dcor = FALSE,
    nscan = 2000,
    burn = 500,
    odens = 25,
    dynamic_beta = "dyad",
    save_log_lik = TRUE,
    verbose = FALSE
)

dim(fit_ll$log_lik) # [n_stored, n_observations]
loo_db <- loo::loo(fit_ll)
print(loo_db)

Run as written, the fit passes the chain comparison and loo() returns elpd_loo = -502.4 (SE 22.7) over the 1050 observed cells, with every Pareto-kk below 0.5. If the matrix would not fit in RAM, save_log_lik = "chunked" streams it to disk (see the forecasting vignette).

loo() and waic() apply to normal, binary, poisson and explicit-cutpoint ordinal (ordinal_cutpoints = "explicit") fits whose observed cells are separate likelihood factors: directed fits with dcor = FALSE, symmetric fits (each unordered dyad counted once) and bipartite fits. fit$log_lik_contract records the scale, observation unit, numerical method and factorization of the saved scores. Capped binary (cbin), fixed-rank nomination (frn) and data-induced ordinal fits, and directed fits with residual dyad correlation, are compared with the goodness-of-fit checks in Comparing Model Specifications below; log_lik_method in ?lame describes the diagnostic scores they can save.

Prior Specifications

The AR(1) coefficients and innovation variances have these default priors:

  • ρuv∼TruncNormal(0.7,0.3,−0.99,0.99)\rho_{uv} \sim \text{TruncNormal}(0.7, 0.3, -0.99, 0.99) for every family, kind and mode. The data see |ρuv||\rho_{uv}| only, so the draws are stored with ρuv≥0\rho_{uv} \ge 0. Explicit rho_uv_mean and rho_uv_sd settings override the default.
  • ρab∼TruncNormal(0.8,0.15,−0.99,0.99)\rho_{ab} \sim \text{TruncNormal}(0.8, 0.15, -0.99, 0.99), slightly less persistent
  • ρβ∼TruncNormal(0.8,0.15,0,0.999)\rho_{\beta} \sim \text{TruncNormal}(0.8, 0.15, 0, 0.999)
  • σuv2/(1−ρuv2)∼InverseGamma(2,1/2)\sigma_{uv}^2 / (1 - \rho_{uv}^2) \sim \text{InverseGamma}(2, 1/2), independently of ρuv\rho_{uv}: the prior is on the stationary variance of a coordinate path, so the innovations shrink as the persistence grows and a persistent path is not pulled toward a lower ρuv\rho_{uv} (prior$uv_var_shape, prior$uv_var_scale; setting sigma_uv_shape or sigma_uv_scale puts the inverse gamma on σuv2\sigma_{uv}^2 itself instead, which the "t" kind keeps as its default, InverseGamma(2,1)\text{InverseGamma}(2, 1)). For the binary, Poisson, ordinal, cbin and frn families the stationary variance is also bounded by prior$uv_var_cap (default 4)
  • σβ2∼InverseGamma(2,1)\sigma_{\beta}^2 \sim \text{InverseGamma}(2, 1)
  • σab2∼InverseGamma(2,s)\sigma_{ab}^2 \sim \text{InverseGamma}(2, s) with a scale ss fixed before sampling. By default it uses the prior mean of the active level variances, mean⁡{ηabSab,0[k,k]/(ηab−3)}\operatorname{mean}\{\eta_{ab} S_{ab,0}[k,k]/(\eta_{ab}-3)\}, times (1−𝚛𝚑𝚘_𝚊𝚋_𝚖𝚎𝚊𝚗2)(1-\texttt{rho\_ab\_mean}^2). Set prior$sigma_ab_scale to supply the scale explicitly, and inspect fit$sigma_ab_prior_scale or prior_summary(fit) for the value used.

All can be customized via the prior argument (e.g. prior = list(rho_beta_mean = ..., sigma_beta_scale = ...)) if you have strong beliefs about the rate of change.

Genuine Dynamics: What They Look Like

We start with an example where dynamics are truly present: 25 actors over 5 periods whose latent positions evolve via an AR(1) with ρ=0.85\rho = 0.85 and innovation SD σuv=0.3\sigma_{uv} = 0.3. Initial positions are drawn at SD 1.5 – above the implied stationary SD of about 0.57 – seeding strong latent structure that drifts toward stationarity, with a negative intercept giving realistic density (roughly 30%).

library(lame)
set.seed(6886)

n_dyn <- 25
n_per <- 5
R_dyn <- 2

# evolving latent positions with AR(1) dynamics
U <- matrix(rnorm(n_dyn * R_dyn, 0, 1.5), n_dyn, R_dyn)
V <- matrix(rnorm(n_dyn * R_dyn, 0, 1.5), n_dyn, R_dyn)

Y_dyn <- list()
for (t in 1:n_per) {
    if (t > 1) {
        U <- 0.85 * U + matrix(rnorm(n_dyn * R_dyn, 0, 0.3), n_dyn, R_dyn)
        V <- 0.85 * V + matrix(rnorm(n_dyn * R_dyn, 0, 0.3), n_dyn, R_dyn)
    }
    eta <- -1 + U %*% t(V)
    Y_t <- matrix(rbinom(n_dyn * n_dyn, 1, pnorm(eta)), n_dyn, n_dyn)
    diag(Y_t) <- NA
    rownames(Y_t) <- colnames(Y_t) <- paste0("A", 1:n_dyn)
    Y_dyn[[t]] <- Y_t
}

# two chains run by default and are compared before the fit is returned
fit_dyn_real <- lame(
    Y_dyn,
    R = 2,
    dynamic_uv = TRUE,
    dynamic_ab = TRUE,
    family = "binary",
    burn = 100,
    nscan = 1000,
    odens = 10,
    verbose = FALSE,
    plot = FALSE
)

summary(fit_dyn_real)
#> 
#> ── Longitudinal AME model summary ──────────────────────────────────────────────
#> 
#> ── Call 
#> Y ~ a[i] + b[j] + rho*e[ji] + U[i,1:2] %*% V[j,1:2], family = 'binary'
#> 
#> ── Model 
#> • Time periods: 5
#> • Family: binary
#> • Mode: unipartite
#> • Dynamic latent positions: enabled (kind = ar1, rho_uv = 0.944)
#> • Dynamic additive effects: enabled (rho_ab = 0.629)
#>   rho_ab: posterior sd 0.105 is 0.83 of the prior sd 0.126: the data barely
#>   inform it.
#> • Dynamic regression coefficients: enabled (kind = rw1)
#> 
#> ── Regression coefficients

#>   reach by chance, if larger.
#> ✔ The chains agree on every monitored quantity (R-hat at most its threshold, with enough effective draws to compare).

The trajectory plot shows how actors move through the latent space. With more than eight actors, pass highlight = a few actor names to colour those paths (ColorBrewer Dark2) and grey out the rest. With genuine temporal structure, the highlighted paths trace short, coherent arcs rather than random jumps:

uv_plot(
    fit_dyn_real,
    plot_type = "trajectory",
    highlight = c("A1", "A5", "A10", "A15")
)

lame() ran two independently seeded chains and compared them before returning the fit: the last line of the summary above reports that they agree on every monitored quantity, and fit_dyn_real$rhat holds the R-hat and effective draws of each. trace_plot() shows the same chains. Under the binary (probit) family the error variance ve is fixed at 1 for identification, so exclude it by its display label:

trace_plot(fit_dyn_real, exclude = "Error variance")

What Happens Without Temporal Structure?

To see how the dynamic model behaves when there is no signal, we fit the same model to independent networks – a null baseline showing what the prior alone produces when the data are uninformative.

set.seed(6886)
n <- 30
n_periods <- 5

# independent binary networks with no temporal structure
Y_list <- list()
for (t in 1:n_periods) {
    Y_t <- matrix(rbinom(n * n, 1, 0.2), n, n)
    diag(Y_t) <- NA
    rownames(Y_t) <- colnames(Y_t) <- paste0("Actor", 1:n)
    Y_list[[t]] <- Y_t
}

# a tight prior on rho_uv to show prior sensitivity
prior_custom <- list(
    rho_uv_mean = 0.95, # expect very slow change in latent positions
    rho_uv_sd = 0.05 # tight prior
)

fit_null <- lame(
    Y = Y_list,
    R = 2,
    dynamic_uv = TRUE,
    dynamic_ab = TRUE,
    family = "binary",
    prior = prior_custom,
    burn = 100,
    nscan = 1000,
    odens = 10,
    # keep per-draw latent trajectories for procrustes_align(per_draw = TRUE)
    posterior_opts = list(save_UV = TRUE),
    verbose = FALSE,
    plot = FALSE
)

summary(fit_null)
#> 
#> ── Longitudinal AME model summary ──────────────────────────────────────────────
#> 
#> ── Call 
#> Y ~ a[i] + b[j] + rho*e[ji] + U[i,1:2] %*% V[j,1:2], family = 'binary'

#>   the credible intervals.

We can compare the estimated persistence parameters across the two settings:

cat("Independent data rho_uv:", round(mean(fit_null$rho_uv), 3), "\n")
#> Independent data rho_uv: 0.918
cat("Correlated data rho_uv:", round(mean(fit_dyn_real$rho_uv), 3), "\n")
#> Correlated data rho_uv: 0.944

The correlated fit used the default prior, centred at 0.7, and the data moved the posterior mean of rho_uv up to 0.94. The independent networks carry no period-to-period correlation, so the posterior of rho_uv there (mean 0.92) keeps the spread of the tight prior it was given, and summary(fit_null) says so: the data barely inform it. Read rho_uv together with that line of the summary and with the trajectory plots (compare the coherent paths above with the erratic paths below).

Visualizing the Null Case

The trajectory plot for independent data looks different. Using the same highlight device as above, the highlighted paths jump from period to period without persistent direction, and the whole cloud clumps near the origin:

uv_plot(
    fit_null,
    plot_type = "trajectory",
    highlight = c("Actor1", "Actor5", "Actor10", "Actor15")
)

The additive effects behave the same way: trajectories reflecting noise rather than real shifts in actor activity.

ab_plot(fit_null, effect = "sender", plot_type = "trajectory")
#> ℹ Showing top 5 and bottom 5 actors by average effect
#> → Use `show_actors` to specify actors to display

Comparing Model Specifications

A natural workflow is to fit several specifications and compare their goodness-of-fit. We use the independent data from above, where dynamic effects should add nothing.

# the four specifications on the same data
fit_static <- lame(
    Y_list,
    R = 2,
    family = "binary",
    burn = 30,
    nscan = 150,
    odens = 5,
    verbose = FALSE,
    plot = FALSE
)

fit_uv <- lame(
    Y_list,
    R = 2,
    dynamic_uv = TRUE,
    family = "binary",
    burn = 30,
    nscan = 150,
    odens = 5,
    verbose = FALSE,
    plot = FALSE
)

fit_ab <- lame(
    Y_list,
    R = 2,
    dynamic_ab = TRUE,
    family = "binary",
    burn = 30,
    nscan = 150,
    odens = 5,
    verbose = FALSE,
    plot = FALSE
)

fit_full <- lame(
    Y_list,
    R = 2,
    dynamic_uv = TRUE,
    dynamic_ab = TRUE,
    family = "binary",
    burn = 30,
    nscan = 150,
    odens = 5,
    verbose = FALSE,
    plot = FALSE
)

For each specification we compute posterior predictive p-values (how often simulated statistics exceed observed): values near 0.5 indicate good fit; values pinned near 0 or 1 flag a statistic the model systematically under- or over-generates.

# posterior predictive p-values for each GOF statistic
compute_pvals <- function(fit) {
    gof <- fit$GOF
    sapply(names(gof), function(stat) {
        mat <- gof[[stat]]
        obs <- mat[, 1] # first column = observed
        sims <- mat[, -1] # remaining = posterior predictive
        mean(colMeans(sims) >= mean(obs))
    })
}

gof_comparison <- rbind(
    Static = compute_pvals(fit_static),
    Dynamic_UV = compute_pvals(fit_uv),
    Dynamic_AB = compute_pvals(fit_ab),
    Full = compute_pvals(fit_full)
)
round(gof_comparison, 3)
#>            sd.rowmean sd.colmean dyad.dep cycle.dep trans.dep
#> Static          0.900      0.983    0.517     0.600     0.250
#> Dynamic_UV      0.900      0.950    0.567     0.583     0.400
#> Dynamic_AB      0.917      1.000    0.617     0.600     0.267
#> Full            1.000      1.000    0.583     0.567     0.467

sd.rowmean and sd.colmean sit near 1 for every specification: the data were generated without actor heterogeneity, and all four models carry additive effects. The specifications are compared on the dyad.dep, cycle.dep, and trans.dep columns. There every value lies between 0.25 and 0.62, away from 0 and 1: each specification reproduces the dependence statistics, and the dynamic terms add nothing to the static fit, as expected for data generated without temporal structure. The same four fits at nscan = 2000, burn = 500, odens = 25 give values between 0.28 and 0.56 in those three columns.

When to Use Dynamic Effects

Use dynamic_ab when actors’ overall activity levels change over time: countries cycle through isolationist and interventionist periods, users churn in and out of platforms.

Use dynamic_uv when the underlying community structure is shifting – a stronger claim: not just that actors are more or less active, but that who connects with whom is changing (political realignment, generational turnover).

Use dynamic_beta when a covariate’s effect on tie formation changes over time while actors and community structure are stable: the question is how strongly X translates into Y, not who is connecting (dynamic_uv) or who is active (dynamic_ab).

Use multiple together when several types of change happen at once. This is the most flexible specification and the one that asks most of the data; summary() says so when the data leave a persistence parameter close to its prior.

Stick with static when you have few time periods, when the network is genuinely stable, or when you primarily care about average covariate effects.

Dealing with Rotational Indeterminacy

One subtlety of dynamic latent space models: the latent space is only identified up to an orthogonal rotation at each time point and at each posterior draw, so averaging raw draws would shrink the positions toward zero. lame() therefore reports positions that factor each period’s posterior mean product UtVt′U_t V_t', the identified quantity, and matches each period to the one before by rotations that leave the product unchanged. procrustes_align() applies the orthogonal-Procrustes rotation (Gower 1975) to align each period’s positions to the previous one; on these positions it changes nothing:

# align latent positions across time
aligned <- procrustes_align(fit_null)
str(aligned$U) # 3D array: actors x dimensions x time
#>  num [1:30, 1:2, 1:5] -0.1774 0.3193 0.0303 0.247 0.1278 ...
#>  - attr(*, "dimnames")=List of 3
#>   ..$ : chr [1:30] "Actor1" "Actor10" "Actor11" "Actor12" ...
#>   ..$ : NULL
#>   ..$ : NULL

Rotation indeterminacy is also a per-draw property: procrustes_align(fit, per_draw = TRUE) aligns every saved draw’s trajectory across time (Hoff 2005; Sewell & Chen 2015), using the per-draw cube a dynamic fit stores by default; see ?procrustes_align.

latent_positions(fit, align = TRUE) returns the aligned positions as a tidy data frame ready for ggplot2 (custom trajectory plots, overlaying external events). Because this fit saved its per-draw trajectories, the posterior_sd column is computed from the draws, each matched onto the reported positions, rather than returned as NA:

lp <- latent_positions(fit_null, align = TRUE)
head(lp)
#>     actor dimension time       value posterior_sd type
#> 1  Actor1         1    1 -0.17737198    0.3068586    U
#> 2 Actor10         1    1  0.31926981    0.3378129    U
#> 3 Actor11         1    1  0.03030389    0.2892598    U
#> 4 Actor12         1    1  0.24701875    0.3355953    U
#> 5 Actor13         1    1  0.12780311    0.3441998    U
#> 6 Actor14         1    1 -0.07995805    0.2965998    U

References

  1. Hoff, PD (2021). Additive and Multiplicative Effects Network Models. Statistical Science 36, 34–50.

  2. Hoff, PD (2005). Bilinear mixed-effects models for dyadic data. Journal of the American Statistical Association 100(469), 286–295.

  3. Sewell, D. K., & Chen, Y. (2015). Latent space models for dynamic networks. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 110(512), 1646-1657.

  4. Carter, C. K., & Kohn, R. (1994). On Gibbs sampling for state space models. Biometrika 81(3), 541–553. The FFBS algorithm behind dynamic_beta_kind = "ar1" / "rw1".

  5. Gower, J. C. (1975). Generalized Procrustes analysis. Psychometrika 40(1), 33–51. The orthogonal-Procrustes rotation underlying procrustes_align().
